title: What a Bubble Does to a Monolayer
source_visual_limits: A published cell-monolayer experiment, not patient airway footage. Flow-device photos, live/dead assay, and actin figure are all the same paper.
human_review: NOT APPROVED — listen, watch, verify panel identities and licensing before live embed
narrator: Kokoro ONNX, synthetic, not a real researcher narration

headline: THE BUBBLE
PASSES.
chapters.narration: A fluid interface crosses a layer of lung epithelial cells. This is the real chamber study, not a film of a patient's lung.

headline: THE REAL
CHAMBER
chapters.narration: A syringe pump drives liquid through a parallel plate chamber. The paper shows the actual apparatus and the glass surfaces supporting the cells.

headline: WHERE STRESS
APPEARS
chapters.narration: As the air liquid interface advances, local stresses reach the cell surface. The moving schematic explains the process; it is not a measured stress trace.

headline: CONTROL
VERSUS BUBBLE
chapters.narration: These fluorescence images are from the original study. The unstressed control and the bubble exposed cells were stained with live and dead markers.

headline: AROUND 53%
CELL DEATH
chapters.narration: Across seven replicates, the stressed group showed about fifty three percent cell death, versus around zero to point two percent in controls. The difference was statistically significant.

headline: LOOK AGAIN AT
THE ACTIN
chapters.narration: The study also stained actin filaments and nuclei. Here are its actual control and bubble exposure images, not synthetic fluorescence pictures.

headline: NO SIGNIFICANT
ACTIN DIFFERENCE
chapters.narration: The single bubble did not produce a statistically significant change in actin organization, although the authors observed possible differences in filament orientation.

headline: ONE MODEL.
ONE QUESTION.
chapters.eyebrow: PUBLISHED METHOD · NOT A PATIENT OUTCOME
chapters.narration: The chamber makes an airway reopening problem experimentally observable. It does not by itself establish what will happen to a patient during ventilation.
